questions.text: In which year, traditionally known as the Year of the Elephant, was Prophet Muhammad (PBUH) born?
questions.explanation: Prophet Muhammad (PBUH) was born in Mecca in 570 CE, the year an Abyssinian army with elephants attempted to attack the Kaaba.

questions.text: What was the name of Prophet Muhammad's (PBUH) father?
questions.explanation: The Prophet's father, Abdullah ibn Abdul Muttalib, died before his birth.

questions.text: What was the name of Prophet Muhammad's (PBUH) mother?
questions.explanation: Aminah bint Wahb was the Prophet's mother; she died when he was about six years old.

questions.text: Who was the foster mother who nursed Prophet Muhammad (PBUH) in his infancy?
questions.explanation: Halima Sa'diyya of the Banu Sa'd tribe nursed and raised the infant Prophet in the desert, following Meccan custom.

questions.text: After the death of his mother, who took charge of raising the young Prophet Muhammad (PBUH)?
questions.explanation: His grandfather Abdul Muttalib cared for him after Aminah's death, until his own death two years later.

questions.text: After his grandfather's death, which uncle became the guardian of Prophet Muhammad (PBUH)?
questions.explanation: Abu Talib, the Prophet's paternal uncle, raised and protected him, including during the early years of his prophethood.

questions.text: Before his prophethood, Prophet Muhammad (PBUH) was widely known among the Meccans by which title for his honesty?
questions.explanation: He was called Al-Amin, meaning 'the Trustworthy', because of his reputation for honesty even before receiving revelation.

questions.text: Who was the first wife of Prophet Muhammad (PBUH)?
questions.explanation: Khadija bint Khuwaylid, a wealthy Meccan merchant, married the Prophet and remained his only wife until her death.

questions.text: At what age did Prophet Muhammad (PBUH) receive his first revelation?
questions.explanation: The Prophet was 40 years old when he received the first revelation in the Cave of Hira.

questions.text: Who was the first woman to accept Islam?
questions.explanation: Khadija, the Prophet's wife, was the first person of any gender to believe in his message.

questions.text: Who was the first child to accept Islam?
questions.explanation: Ali ibn Abi Talib, the Prophet's young cousin living in his household, is traditionally regarded as the first child to accept Islam.

questions.text: Who was the first freed slave to accept Islam?
questions.explanation: Zaid bin Haritha, adopted into the Prophet's household, was the first among the freed slaves to embrace Islam.

questions.text: Who was the first free adult man to accept Islam?
questions.explanation: Abu Bakr, a close friend of the Prophet, is regarded as the first free adult male to accept Islam.

questions.text: During the early Meccan period, on which hill did Prophet Muhammad (PBUH) first publicly call the Quraysh to Islam?
questions.explanation: The Prophet gathered the Quraysh at Mount Safa to deliver his first open, public call to Islam.

questions.text: Persecuted Muslims in Mecca were advised by Prophet Muhammad (PBUH) to migrate for refuge to which kingdom?
questions.explanation: The Prophet sent a group of early Muslims to Abyssinia (Christian Ethiopia), known for its just ruler, to escape Meccan persecution.

questions.text: Who was the ruler of Abyssinia who gave refuge to the early Muslim migrants?
questions.explanation: The Negus, known in Arabic sources as An-Najashi, protected the Muslim migrants and refused to hand them over to the Quraysh.

questions.text: Which year of Prophet Muhammad's (PBUH) life is known as 'Aam-ul-Huzn' (the Year of Sorrow), marked by the deaths of Khadija and Abu Talib?
questions.explanation: The tenth year of prophethood brought the deaths of both Khadija and Abu Talib in close succession, hence the name 'Year of Sorrow'.

questions.text: The night journey of Prophet Muhammad (PBUH) from Masjid al-Haram to Masjid al-Aqsa is known as
questions.explanation: Al-Isra refers to the miraculous night journey from Mecca to Jerusalem, which preceded the ascension (Miraj).

questions.text: During the Miraj (ascension), how many daily prayers were made obligatory upon Muslims?
questions.explanation: Although fifty prayers were initially prescribed, the number was eventually reduced to five obligatory daily prayers.

questions.text: The first pledge of Aqabah was taken between Prophet Muhammad (PBUH) and a group of people from which city?
questions.explanation: Pilgrims from Yathrib met the Prophet at Aqabah near Mina and pledged to accept Islam, paving the way for the later Hijrah.

questions.text: In which Gregorian year did the Hijrah (migration) of Prophet Muhammad (PBUH) from Mecca to Medina take place?
questions.explanation: The Hijrah took place in 622 CE and later became the starting point of the Islamic lunar calendar.

questions.text: Who accompanied Prophet Muhammad (PBUH) during the migration (Hijrah) to Medina?
questions.explanation: Abu Bakr accompanied the Prophet on the journey to Medina, sharing the risks of the migration with him.

questions.text: In which cave did Prophet Muhammad (PBUH) and Abu Bakr take shelter during the Hijrah?
questions.explanation: They hid for three days in the Cave of Thawr, south of Mecca, before continuing on to Medina.

questions.text: Which was the first mosque built by Prophet Muhammad (PBUH), on the outskirts of Medina during the Hijrah?
questions.explanation: Masjid Quba was built just outside Medina and is regarded as the first mosque established in Islam.

questions.text: In Medina, Prophet Muhammad (PBUH) paired each migrant (Muhajir) with a local Ansari as brothers; this bond is known as
questions.explanation: The Mawakhat (bond of brotherhood) linked Muhajireen and Ansar as brothers, helping the migrants settle in Medina.

questions.text: In which year after Hijrah did the Battle of Badr take place?
questions.explanation: The Battle of Badr, the first major battle between the Muslims and the Meccan Quraysh, was fought in 2 AH.

questions.text: At the Battle of Badr, the Muslim army was heavily outnumbered by the Meccan Quraysh; the Muslims numbered approximately
questions.explanation: The Muslim force at Badr numbered around 313 men against a much larger Quraysh army.

questions.text: In which year after Hijrah did the Battle of Uhud take place?
questions.explanation: The Battle of Uhud was fought in 3 AH, a year after the Muslim victory at Badr.

questions.text: The Muslim setback at the Battle of Uhud is chiefly attributed to which action?
options: Archers leaving their assigned position on the hill
The Muslims being outnumbered ten to one
The Prophet's absence from the battlefield
A shortage of weapons among the Muslims
questions.explanation: A group of archers left their post to gather spoils, exposing the Muslim rear and allowing the Quraysh cavalry to turn the battle.

questions.text: Who suggested digging a trench around Medina to defend against the confederate forces in 5 AH?
questions.explanation: Salman al-Farsi, familiar with Persian military tactics, proposed digging a trench to defend Medina.

questions.text: The Battle of the Trench is also known as
questions.explanation: The Battle of the Trench is also called Khandaq or Al-Ahzab, referring to the confederate tribes that besieged Medina.

questions.text: In which year after Hijrah was the Treaty of Hudaybiyyah signed between the Muslims and the Quraysh?
questions.explanation: The Treaty of Hudaybiyyah was signed in 6 AH, establishing a ten-year truce between the Muslims and the Quraysh.

questions.text: In which year after Hijrah did the peaceful conquest of Mecca take place?
questions.explanation: Mecca was conquered largely without bloodshed in 8 AH after the Quraysh violated the Treaty of Hudaybiyyah.

questions.text: At the conquest of Mecca, Prophet Muhammad (PBUH) ordered the removal of how many idols from around the Kaaba, according to tradition?
questions.explanation: Tradition holds that 360 idols surrounding the Kaaba were destroyed on the Prophet's orders after the conquest of Mecca.

questions.text: Shortly after the conquest of Mecca, Muslim forces fought a confederation of Bedouin tribes at
questions.explanation: The Battle of Hunayn, fought soon after the conquest of Mecca, was against the Hawazin and Thaqif tribal confederation.

questions.text: The last military expedition personally led by Prophet Muhammad (PBUH), directed toward the Byzantine frontier, was the
questions.explanation: The Expedition of Tabuk, undertaken in response to rumours of a Byzantine advance, was the Prophet's final personally-led campaign.

questions.text: In which year after Hijrah did Prophet Muhammad (PBUH) perform his only and Farewell Pilgrimage (Hajjatul Wida)?
questions.explanation: The Prophet performed his only Hajj, known as the Farewell Pilgrimage, in 10 AH.

questions.text: Prophet Muhammad (PBUH) delivered his Farewell Sermon at
questions.explanation: The Farewell Sermon was delivered on Mount Arafat during the Farewell Pilgrimage, setting out key principles of Islamic conduct.

questions.text: In which year after Hijrah did Prophet Muhammad (PBUH) pass away?
questions.explanation: The Prophet passed away in Medina in 11 AH, shortly after completing the Farewell Pilgrimage.

questions.text: Prophet Muhammad (PBUH) is buried in Medina, in the chamber that had belonged to which of his wives?
questions.explanation: The Prophet was buried in the room of his wife Aisha, adjoining Masjid-e-Nabvi in Medina.

questions.text: Who was appointed by Prophet Muhammad (PBUH) as the first muezzin to call the adhan?
questions.explanation: Bilal ibn Rabah, a freed Abyssinian slave known for his beautiful voice, was chosen as the first muezzin in Islam.

questions.text: Which uncle of Prophet Muhammad (PBUH), titled 'Lion of Allah', was martyred at the Battle of Uhud?
questions.explanation: Hamza ibn Abdul Muttalib, called Asadullah (Lion of Allah), was killed at Uhud and is remembered as a chief martyr of Islam.

questions.text: In which year after Hijrah was the direction of prayer (Qibla) changed from Jerusalem to the Kaaba?
questions.explanation: The Qibla was changed from Jerusalem to the Kaaba in Mecca in 2 AH, while the Prophet was praying in Medina.

questions.text: Which companion, later known as 'Saifullah' (the Sword of Allah), commanded the Muslim army after the death of its three commanders at the Battle of Mu'tah?
questions.explanation: Khalid bin Waleed took command at Mu'tah after the deaths of Zaid bin Haritha, Ja'far ibn Abi Talib, and Abdullah ibn Rawaha, and skilfully led the army's withdrawal.

questions.text: Prophet Muhammad's (PBUH) mosque in Medina, built after the Hijrah, is known as
questions.explanation: Masjid-e-Nabvi, built by the Prophet in Medina, became the central mosque of the early Muslim community.

questions.text: The declaration 'La ilaha illallah Muhammadur Rasulullah' is known as
questions.explanation: The Shahada is the testimony of faith affirming the oneness of God and the prophethood of Muhammad (PBUH), the first pillar of Islam.

questions.text: According to Islamic law, Salah becomes obligatory on a Muslim upon reaching
questions.explanation: Salah becomes obligatory once a Muslim of sound mind reaches puberty, though children are encouraged to practice it earlier.

questions.text: How many obligatory (fard) prayers must a Muslim offer each day?
questions.explanation: Muslims are obligated to perform five daily prayers: Fajr, Zuhr, Asr, Maghrib, and Isha.

questions.text: Which of the five daily prayers consists of only two obligatory rakats?
questions.explanation: Fajr, the dawn prayer, consists of two obligatory rakats, fewer than the other daily prayers.

questions.text: Muslims face which direction while performing Salah?
questions.explanation: Muslims face the Kaaba in Mecca, the Qibla, during Salah, a direction fixed since the second year after Hijrah.

questions.text: The ritual ablution performed before Salah is called
questions.explanation: Wudu is the ritual washing of the face, arms, head, and feet performed before Salah.

questions.text: When water is unavailable or unsafe to use, a Muslim may perform ritual purification using clean earth or sand; this is called
questions.explanation: Tayammum is a dry ablution using clean earth, permitted when water is unavailable, insufficient, or harmful to use.

questions.text: Zakat is obligatory on a Muslim's wealth once it equals or exceeds a minimum threshold known as
questions.explanation: Nisab is the minimum amount of wealth a Muslim must own before Zakat becomes obligatory.

questions.text: The standard rate of Zakat payable on qualifying savings and cash held for a full lunar year is
questions.explanation: Zakat on savings and cash is generally calculated at 2.5% of the qualifying wealth.

questions.text: Zakat becomes obligatory on savings after they remain in a Muslim's possession, above the nisab, for
questions.explanation: Zakat is due once qualifying wealth above the nisab has been held for one complete lunar (Hijri) year.

questions.text: Fasting (Sawm) is obligatory on Muslims during which month of the Islamic calendar?
questions.explanation: Sawm, obligatory fasting from dawn to sunset, is observed throughout the month of Ramadan.

questions.text: The pre-dawn meal eaten before beginning the daily fast in Ramadan is called
questions.explanation: Suhoor is the meal taken before dawn, prior to starting the day's fast.

questions.text: The meal with which a fasting Muslim breaks the fast at sunset is called
questions.explanation: Iftar is the meal eaten at sunset to end the day's fast during Ramadan.

questions.text: Performing Hajj is obligatory once in a lifetime on every adult Muslim who meets the condition of
questions.explanation: Hajj is obligatory only on those who possess Istita'ah, meaning the physical health and financial means to undertake the journey.

questions.text: The sacred state of consecration a pilgrim enters before performing Hajj or Umrah, marked by wearing simple unstitched garments, is called
questions.explanation: Ihram is the state of ritual consecration a pilgrim enters, symbolised for men by wearing two plain unstitched sheets.

questions.text: Hajj is performed during which Islamic month?
questions.explanation: Hajj takes place during the first ten days of Dhul Hijjah, the final month of the Islamic calendar.

questions.text: The ritual of circling the Kaaba seven times during Hajj or Umrah is called
questions.explanation: Tawaf is the ritual circumambulation of the Kaaba, performed seven times in a counter-clockwise direction.

questions.text: The ritual of walking briskly seven times between the hills of Safa and Marwah during Hajj or Umrah is called
questions.explanation: Sa'i commemorates Hajar's search for water and involves walking between Safa and Marwah seven times.

questions.text: The symbolic stoning of pillars during Hajj, commemorating the rejection of Satan's temptation, is called
questions.explanation: Ramy al-Jamarat involves throwing pebbles at three pillars in Mina, symbolising the rejection of Satan.

questions.text: Unlike Hajj, which can only be performed at a fixed time of year, the minor pilgrimage that may be performed at any time is called
questions.explanation: Umrah is a shorter, non-obligatory pilgrimage to Mecca that may be performed at any point during the year.

questions.text: Which of the following correctly lists the Five Pillars of Islam?
questions.explanation: The Five Pillars are Shahada, Salah, Zakat, Sawm, and Hajj, the core obligatory acts of Islamic practice.

questions.text: Which four schools of Fiqh (jurisprudence) are recognized within Sunni Islam?
questions.explanation: The four major Sunni schools of jurisprudence are Hanafi, Maliki, Shafi'i, and Hanbali.

questions.text: The Hanafi school of Fiqh was founded by
questions.explanation: Imam Abu Hanifa founded the Hanafi school, which is the most widely followed school of Fiqh in South Asia.

questions.text: The Maliki school of Fiqh takes its name from
questions.explanation: The Maliki school is named after Imam Malik ibn Anas of Medina, author of the Muwatta.

questions.text: The Shafi'i school of Fiqh was founded by
questions.explanation: Imam Muhammad ibn Idris al-Shafi'i founded the Shafi'i school, known for systematising the principles of Islamic jurisprudence.

questions.text: The Hanbali school of Fiqh takes its name from
questions.explanation: The Hanbali school is named after Imam Ahmad ibn Hanbal, also known for his hadith compilation, the Musnad.

questions.text: Which school of Fiqh is predominantly followed by Muslims in Pakistan?
questions.explanation: The Hanafi school is the predominant school of Fiqh followed by the majority of Muslims in Pakistan.

questions.text: In Islamic jurisprudence, an act that is obligatory and whose omission is sinful is termed
questions.explanation: Fard denotes an act that is obligatory in Islamic law, such as the five daily prayers.

questions.text: An act that the Prophet (PBUH) regularly practised but which is not strictly obligatory is termed
questions.explanation: Sunnah refers to practices regularly followed by the Prophet (PBUH), recommended though not strictly obligatory.

questions.text: According to the Hanafi school, the Witr prayer is generally regarded as
questions.explanation: The Hanafi school considers Witr, offered after Isha, to be Wajib (necessary), distinguishing it from the other schools' views.

questions.text: The congregational Friday prayer, obligatory on adult male Muslims, is called
questions.explanation: Salat-ul-Jumu'ah is the obligatory congregational prayer performed by adult male Muslims on Fridays.

questions.text: The Friday congregational prayer replaces which of the five daily obligatory prayers?
questions.explanation: Jumu'ah prayer is performed in place of the Zuhr prayer on Fridays.

questions.text: The charity that must be given by every Muslim before the Eid-ul-Fitr prayer is called
questions.explanation: Sadaqah-tul-Fitr, also called Fitrana, must be given before the Eid-ul-Fitr prayer to ensure the needy can also celebrate.

questions.text: The animal sacrifice performed by Muslims during Eid-ul-Adha, commemorating Prophet Ibrahim's willingness to sacrifice his son, is called
questions.explanation: Qurbani is the ritual animal sacrifice performed during Eid-ul-Adha in remembrance of Prophet Ibrahim's obedience.

questions.text: The practice of retreating into a mosque for devotion, especially observed during the last ten days of Ramadan, is called
questions.explanation: I'tikaf is a period of spiritual seclusion in the mosque, commonly observed during the last ten days of Ramadan.

questions.text: Who became the first Caliph of Islam after the death of Prophet Muhammad (PBUH)?
questions.explanation: Abu Bakr was chosen as the first Caliph following the Prophet's death in 11 AH.

questions.text: Abu Bakr is generally known by the title
questions.explanation: Abu Bakr was given the title As-Siddiq (the Truthful) for his immediate belief in the Prophet's night journey and message.

questions.text: The wars fought by Caliph Abu Bakr against tribes that renounced Islam or refused to pay Zakat after the Prophet's death are known as
questions.explanation: The Ridda Wars were fought by Abu Bakr to suppress tribal rebellion and apostasy that broke out after the Prophet's death.

questions.text: During the Ridda Wars, Muslim forces under Khalid bin Waleed defeated the false prophet Musaylimah at the
questions.explanation: Khalid bin Waleed defeated Musaylimah's forces at the Battle of Yamama, ending one of the major Ridda rebellions.

questions.text: The compilation of the Quran into a single written volume was first undertaken during the caliphate of
questions.explanation: After many Quran reciters died in the Ridda Wars, Abu Bakr ordered the first compilation of the Quran into one volume.

questions.text: Who was entrusted with compiling the written Quran into a single volume during Abu Bakr's caliphate?
questions.explanation: Zaid ibn Thabit, a scribe of revelation, was tasked with collecting the Quran into a single written text.

questions.text: Abu Bakr's caliphate lasted approximately
questions.explanation: Abu Bakr ruled as Caliph for about two years, from 632 to 634 CE.

questions.text: Before becoming Caliph, Abu Bakr was the father-in-law of Prophet Muhammad (PBUH) through his daughter
questions.explanation: Abu Bakr's daughter Aisha married the Prophet, making Abu Bakr his father-in-law.

questions.text: Abu Bakr nominated which companion as his successor before his death?
questions.explanation: Before his death, Abu Bakr nominated Umar ibn al-Khattab as the next Caliph.

questions.text: Caliph Abu Bakr is buried in Medina beside
questions.explanation: Abu Bakr is buried next to Prophet Muhammad (PBUH) in the chamber that had belonged to Aisha.

questions.text: The second Rightly-Guided Caliph, Umar ibn al-Khattab, is commonly known by the title
questions.explanation: Umar ibn al-Khattab was given the title Al-Farooq, meaning one who distinguishes truth from falsehood.

questions.text: Caliph Umar ibn al-Khattab was assassinated by
options: Abu Lu'lu'ah Firoz, a Persian slave
questions.explanation: Umar was fatally stabbed by Abu Lu'lu'ah Firoz, a Persian slave, while leading the Fajr prayer.

questions.text: The Islamic (Hijri) lunar calendar, taking the migration to Medina as its starting point, was formally adopted during the caliphate of
questions.explanation: Umar ibn al-Khattab formally established the Hijri calendar, dating years from the Prophet's migration to Medina.

questions.text: The decisive battle in which Muslim forces defeated the Sassanid Persian army, opening the way to Iraq, was the Battle of
questions.explanation: The Battle of Qadisiyyah broke Sassanid resistance in Iraq and opened the way for the Muslim conquest of Persia.

questions.text: The battle that broke the main Byzantine resistance in Syria, fought in 636 CE, was the Battle of
questions.explanation: The Battle of Yarmouk, fought in 636 CE, decisively broke Byzantine power in Syria.

questions.text: The battle sometimes called the 'Victory of Victories', which broke organized Sassanid resistance in Persia, was the Battle of
questions.explanation: The Battle of Nahavand, fought under Umar's caliphate, is often called the 'Victory of Victories' for ending organized Persian resistance.

questions.text: When Caliph Umar entered Jerusalem in 637 CE, he granted its Christian inhabitants a covenant guaranteeing their safety and property; this is known as
questions.explanation: The Covenant of Umar guaranteed the safety, property, and freedom of worship of Jerusalem's Christian population.

questions.text: Umar ibn al-Khattab was the first Caliph to adopt the title
questions.explanation: Umar was the first to be addressed as Amir-ul-Momineen, meaning Commander of the Faithful.

questions.text: Caliph Umar's administrative reforms included establishing a public treasury known as
questions.explanation: Umar formally organized the Bait-ul-Mal, a public treasury used to administer state revenues and distribute stipends.

questions.text: Umar ibn al-Khattab's caliphate lasted approximately
questions.explanation: Umar ruled as Caliph for about ten years, from 634 to 644 CE, during which the Islamic state expanded rapidly.

questions.text: Before his death, Caliph Umar appointed a council to choose his successor from among its members; this council is known as
questions.explanation: Umar appointed a six-member Shura council to select the next Caliph from among themselves after his death.

questions.text: The third Rightly-Guided Caliph, Uthman ibn Affan, is known by the title 'Dhun-Nurayn' (Possessor of Two Lights) because he married
options: Two of the Prophet's daughters, successively
questions.explanation: Uthman married the Prophet's daughters Ruqayyah and, after her death, Umm Kulthum, earning him the title Dhun-Nurayn.

questions.text: Caliph Uthman ibn Affan is chiefly remembered for
options: Compiling the first written copy of the Quran
Standardizing the text of the Quran into a single authoritative copy
questions.explanation: Uthman is best remembered for standardizing the Quran's text and distributing authoritative copies to major cities.

questions.text: The standardized copies of the Quran prepared under Caliph Uthman are known as
questions.explanation: The standardized copies produced under Uthman are known as the Uthmanic codices, or Mushaf.

questions.text: During his caliphate, Uthman ibn Affan carried out a significant expansion of
questions.explanation: Uthman expanded and rebuilt Masjid-e-Nabvi in Medina to accommodate the growing Muslim community.

questions.text: Uthman ibn Affan's caliphate lasted approximately
questions.explanation: Uthman ruled as Caliph for about twelve years, from 644 to 656 CE.

questions.text: Caliph Uthman ibn Affan was assassinated by
options: Rebels who besieged his house in Medina
questions.explanation: Uthman was killed by rebels who besieged his house in Medina and forced their way in while he was reading the Quran.

questions.text: Caliph Uthman ibn Affan is credited with establishing the first organized
questions.explanation: Uthman authorized the building of the first organized Muslim naval fleet, used in campaigns such as the conquest of Cyprus.

questions.text: The fourth Rightly-Guided Caliph, Ali ibn Abi Talib, was married to Prophet Muhammad's (PBUH) daughter
questions.explanation: Ali ibn Abi Talib was married to Fatima, the Prophet's youngest daughter.

questions.text: Caliph Ali ibn Abi Talib moved the seat of the caliphate from Medina to
questions.explanation: Ali relocated the capital of the caliphate to Kufa in present-day Iraq.

questions.text: The battle fought between Caliph Ali and a force led by Aisha, Talha, and Zubayr is known as the
questions.explanation: The Battle of the Camel, named for the camel Aisha rode during the fighting, was fought between Ali's forces and those of Aisha, Talha, and Zubayr.

questions.text: The battle fought between the forces of Caliph Ali and Muawiyah ibn Abi Sufyan in 657 CE is known as the
questions.explanation: The Battle of Siffin was fought between Ali's forces and those of Muawiyah, ending inconclusively with an arbitration agreement.

questions.text: The group that broke away from Ali's camp after rejecting the arbitration following the Battle of Siffin became known as the
questions.explanation: The Kharijites rejected the outcome of the arbitration after Siffin and turned against both Ali and Muawiyah.

questions.text: Caliph Ali ibn Abi Talib was assassinated by
options: A Kharijite, Abdur Rahman ibn Muljam
questions.explanation: Ali was fatally wounded by the Kharijite Abdur Rahman ibn Muljam while praying in the mosque at Kufa.

questions.text: Ali ibn Abi Talib's caliphate lasted approximately
questions.explanation: Ali ruled as Caliph for about five years, from 656 to 661 CE, a period marked by internal conflict.

questions.text: The four Caliphs who ruled after Prophet Muhammad (PBUH), regarded as having followed his example most closely, are collectively called
questions.explanation: Abu Bakr, Umar, Uthman, and Ali are together known as the Khulafa-e-Rashideen, the Rightly-Guided Caliphs.

questions.text: The correct chronological order of the four Rightly-Guided Caliphs is
questions.explanation: The Rightly-Guided Caliphs ruled in the order Abu Bakr, Umar, Uthman, and then Ali.

questions.text: The era of the Rightly-Guided Caliphs came to an end and was succeeded by which dynasty, established by Muawiyah ibn Abi Sufyan?
questions.explanation: After Ali's death, Muawiyah ibn Abi Sufyan established the Umayyad dynasty, ending the Rashidun era.

questions.text: Taken together, the reigns of the four Rightly-Guided Caliphs spanned a total of approximately
questions.explanation: From Abu Bakr's accession in 632 CE to Ali's death in 661 CE, the Rashidun era lasted about 29 years.

questions.text: Under which Caliph was the conquest of the Sassanid Persian Empire substantially completed?
questions.explanation: The decisive victories at Qadisiyyah and Nahavand under Umar's caliphate broke organized Sassanid resistance in Persia.

questions.text: The branch of philosophy concerned with moral principles that govern a person's behaviour is called
questions.explanation: Ethics is the study of moral principles that determine right and wrong conduct.

questions.text: Regularly paying one's taxes and obeying the law of the land are examples of
questions.explanation: Paying taxes and obeying the law are basic civic responsibilities expected of every citizen.

questions.text: An awareness of one's duties toward the community and public property, such as keeping public spaces clean, is generally described as
questions.explanation: Civic sense refers to an individual's awareness of and respect for shared community responsibilities and public property.

questions.text: The principle that no one, including the government, is above the law, and that all are treated equally under it, is known as
questions.explanation: The rule of law holds that all individuals and institutions, including the state, are subject to and equal before the law.

questions.text: Unlike laws, which are enforced by the state, moral principles concerning right and wrong conduct are primarily enforced through
questions.explanation: Moral principles are generally upheld through personal conscience and social approval or disapproval, rather than formal legal enforcement.

questions.text: A system of government in which political power ultimately rests with the citizens, typically exercised through elected representatives, is called
questions.explanation: Democracy is a system of government in which power ultimately rests with the citizens, usually exercised through elected representatives.

questions.text: Basic entitlements guaranteed to every citizen, such as the right to life, equality, and freedom of expression, are known as
questions.explanation: Fundamental rights are basic entitlements guaranteed to citizens, such as the right to life, equality, and free expression.

questions.text: Which of the following is generally considered a duty of a responsible citizen, rather than a right?
options: Obeying the law and respecting the rights of others
questions.explanation: Obeying the law and respecting the rights of others are civic duties expected of citizens, distinct from their guaranteed rights.

questions.text: Accepting and respecting beliefs, practices, and ways of life that differ from one's own, especially in a diverse society, reflects the value of
questions.explanation: Tolerance is the willingness to accept and respect beliefs and practices that differ from one's own.

questions.text: Speaking and acting truthfully, and keeping one's promises, reflects the moral value of
questions.explanation: Honesty and integrity involve consistently speaking the truth and honouring one's commitments.

questions.text: The ethical principle of treating others as one would wish to be treated is commonly known as
questions.explanation: The Golden Rule is the ethical principle of treating others the way one would wish to be treated.

questions.text: Fair and impartial treatment of individuals, ensuring that everyone receives what they are due, defines the value of
questions.explanation: Justice refers to fair and impartial treatment, ensuring individuals receive what is rightfully due to them.

questions.text: The Universal Declaration of Human Rights was adopted by the United Nations General Assembly in
questions.explanation: The Universal Declaration of Human Rights was adopted by the United Nations General Assembly in 1948.

questions.text: The Universal Declaration of Human Rights was adopted by which international body?
questions.explanation: The United Nations General Assembly adopted the Universal Declaration of Human Rights in 1948.

questions.text: Practices such as conserving water, reducing waste, and protecting public parks are examples of
questions.explanation: Conserving resources and protecting shared public spaces are examples of environmental civic responsibility.

questions.text: The misuse of public office or entrusted power for private gain is defined as
questions.explanation: Corruption is the misuse of public office or entrusted authority for personal or private benefit.

questions.explanation: Siddhartha Gautama is traditionally held to have been born in Lumbini, in present-day Nepal.
